readings.c1s1:
¶
2. A messuage; a house and homestead. Also ''toftstead.''

{{smaller block|Worsthorne was the property of Henry de Wrdest, in the reign of Stephen, or Henry II., who granted a ''toft'' and a croft in the vill of Wrdest to Henry the son of Adam de Winhill.
{{right|''Baines'', Hist. Lancashire, II. 38.}}}}

3. In ''Eng. common law:'' (''a'') A messuage the tenant of which is entitled by virtue of it to rights of common in other land in the parish or district.

{{smaller block|A house with its stables and farm-buildings, surrounded by a hedge or inclosure, was called a court, or, as we find it in our law books, a curtilage; the ''toft'' or homestead of a more genuine English dialect.
{{right|''Hallam'', Middle Ages, ix. 1.}}}}

(''b'') A piece of ground on which a messuage formerly stood, and which, though the messuage be gone to decay, is still called by a name indicating something more than mere land.

'''toft'''<sup>2</sup> (tôft), ''n.'' [< ''tuft''<sup>2</sup>.] A grove of trees. ''Bailey'', 1731.

'''toftman''' (tôft′man), ''n.''; pl. ''toftmen'' (-men). [< ''toft''<sup>1</sup> + ''man.''] The owner or occupier of a toft.

'''toftstead''' (tôft′sted), ''n.'' Same as ''toft''<sup>1</sup>, 2.

{{smaller block|The fields are commonable from the 12th of August to the 12th of November to every burgess or occupier of a ''toftstead.''
{{right|''Archæologia'', XLVI. 415.}}}}

'''tofus''', ''n.'' A variant of ''tophus'' for ''toph.''

'''tog'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''tug.''

'''tog'''<sup>2</sup> (tog), ''n.'' [A slang term, perhaps < OF. ''togue, toge'', L. ''toga'', a robe: see ''toge, toga.'' Hence ''tog'', ''v.'', ''togeman'', ''togman'', and ''toggery.'']

readings.c3s2:
¶
'''toggle''' (tog′l), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''toggel'', ''toggil''; appar. a dim. form, connected with ''tug'' (ME. ''toggen''), ''tow''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''tuggle''.] 1. ''Naut.'', a pin placed through the bight or eye of a rope, block-strap, or bolt, to keep it in its place, or to put the bight or eye of another rope upon, and thus secure them both together; also, a pin passed through a link of a chain which is itself passed through a link of the same or a different chain.

{{smaller block|The yard-ropes were fixed to the halter by a ''toggle'' in the running noose of the latter.
{{right|''Marryat'', Frank Mildmay, viii. (''Davies.'')}}}}

2. Two rods or plates hinged together by a toggle-joint: a mechanical device for transmitting force or pressure at a right angle with its direction. See ''toggle-joint'', and cut under ''stone-breaker''.—{{smaller|'''Blubber-toggle''', a blubber-fid (which see, under ''fid'').}}

'''toggle''' (tog′l), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''toggled'', ppr. ''toggling''. [< ''toggle'', ''n.''] To fix or fasten (itself in something) like a toggle-iron; used reflexively, to stick fast.

{{smaller block|A rocket at short range was fired entirely through the body of a whale, and ''toggled itself'' on the side.
{{right|''Fisheries of U. S.'', X. ii. 254.}}}}

'''toggle-bolt''' (tog′l-bōlt), ''n.'' See ''toggle'', 1.

'''toggle-harpoon''' (tog′l-här-pön″), ''n.'' The common toggle-iron.

'''toggle-hole''' (tog′l-hōl), ''n.'' A hole made, as in blubber, for inserting a toggle.

'''toggle-iron''' (tog′l-ī″ėrn), ''n.'' The form of whalers' harpoon now in general use, having a movable blade instead of fixed barbs; the instru-
readings.c3s3: ment used in first striking a whale (when explosives are not employed), for fastening it to the whale-boat by means of a tow-line, so that the boat may be hauled up to the whale, and the latter be killed by hand-lancing at close quarters, or by bomb-lancing at longer range.

This blade has a cutting edge for penetrating the blubber, and a dull back which prevents it from cutting its way out when the line is hauled upon. Also called simply the ''iron.''}}

'''toggle-joint''' (tog′l-joint), ''n.'' In ''mech.'', a joint formed of plates or bars hinged together in such manner that when at rest the
readings.c3s5: two parts form a bend called the ''knuckle;'' an elbow- or knee-joint. {{smaller|It is used by applying power, by means of a screw or a lever, against the knuckle, when the tendency of the two leaves or bars to extend exerts a powerful pressure. This device is much used in printing-presses and other presses. See ''toggle-press.'' See also cuts under ''skate'' and ''stone-breaker.''}}

{{smaller block|It [the toggle] has a hole near one end, through which a rope is attached, which is termed the ''toggle-lanyard.'' This lanyard is used in handling or confining the toggle.

'''toftstead''' (tôft′sted), ''n.'' Same as ''toft''1, 2. {{smaller block|The fields are commonable from the 12th of August to the 12th of November to every burgess or occupier of a ''toftstead.'' {{right|''Archæologia'', XLVI. 415.}}}} '''tofus''', ''n.'' A variant of ''tophus'' for ''toph.'' '''tog'''1†, ''v.'' A Middle English form of ''tug.'' '''tog'''2 (tog), ''n.'' [A slang term, perhaps < OF. ''togue, toge'', L. ''toga'', a robe: see ''toge, toga.'' Hence ''tog'', ''v.'', ''togeman'', ''togman'', and ''toggery.''] A garment: usually in the plural. {{smaller block|Look at his ''togs''—superfine cloth, and the heavy-swell cut! {{right|''Dickens'', Oliver Twist, xvi.}}}} {{smaller block|What did I do but go to church with all my topmost ''togs!'' And that not from respect alone for the parson. {{right|''R. D. Blackmore'', Maid of Sker, vii.}}}} '''Long tog''', a coat. ''Tuft's Glossary of Thieves' Jargon'', 1798.—'''Long togs''' (''naut.''), shore clothes. {{smaller block|I took no "''long togs''" with me; . . . being dressed like the rest, in white duck trousers, blue jacket, and straw hat. {{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 131.}}}} '''tog'''2 (tog), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''togged'', ppr. ''togging''. [< ''tog''2, ''n.''] To dress. [Slang.] {{smaller block|He was ''tog'd'' gnostically enough. {{right|''Scott'', St. Ronan's Well, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|Scrumptious young girls you ''tog'' out so finely, Adorning the diggings so charming and gay. {{right|''Chambers's Journal'', July, 1879, p. 368. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}} '''toga''' (tō′gä̤), ''n.'' [< L. ''toga'', a mantle, lit. a covering, < ''tegere'', cover: see ''tect'', ''tegument''. Cf. ''toge''.] The principal outer garment worn by the ancient Romans. {{smaller|It was a loose and flowing mantle or wrap, of irregular form, in which it differed from the kindred Greek}} garment, the himation, which was rectangular. It was made of wool, or sometimes (under the emperors) of silk, and its usual color was white. It covered the whole body with the exception of the right arm, and the right to wear it was an exclusive privilege of the Roman citizen. The ''toga virilis'', or manly robe, was assumed by Roman youths when they attained the age of fourteen. The ''toga prætexta'', which had a deep purple border, was worn by the children of the nobles, by girls until they were married, and by boys until they were fourteen, when they assumed the toga virilis. It was also the official robe of the higher magistrates, of priests, and of persons discharging {{smaller block|vows. The ''toga picta'' was ornamented with Phrygian embroidery, and was worn by high officers on special occasions, such as the celebration of a triumph. The ''trabea'' was a toga ornamented with horizontal purple stripes; it was the characteristic uniform of the knights (''equites'') upon festival days. Persons accused of any crime allowed their togas to become soiled (''toga sordidata'') as a sign of dejection; candidates for public offices whitened their togas artificially with chalk; while mourners wore a ''toga pulla'' of natural black wool. See also cut in next column.}} [[File:century v08 p0170 c1f1.png|center|193px]] {{c|Roman Toga.—Statue of the Emperor Tiberius.}} '''togaed''' (tō′gäd), ''a.'' [< ''toga'' + ''-ed''2.] Equipped with or clad in a toga. {{smaller block|A couple of ''togaed'' effigies of recent grand-dukes. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Trans. Sketches, p. 316.}}}} '''togated''' (tō′gā-ted), ''a.'' [< L. ''togatus'', wearing or entitled to wear the toga (< ''toga'', toga: see ''toga''), + ''-ed''2.] 1. Dressed in a toga or robe; draped in the classical manner. {{smaller block|FRA, sinus of toga. As worn, point E was placed on the left shoulder, the edge FJ hanging down free in front of the body; the whole of the remainder of the garment was then thrown diagonally around the back, so that ''a'' on the seam of the sinus came under the right elbow, and ''b'' at the middle of the waist in front; the seam was now directed upward, so that the point ''c'' approximately covered E, where the garment first touched the body. The last third of the toga, OPCQ, was thrown over the left shoulder and fell to the ground in voluminous folds, draping the back. The so-called umbo or nodus of the toga was found at F, over the left breast, at the point of junction of the sinus. Point L fell over the left calf, point M over the right, and point N over the left wrist.}} [[File:century v08 p0170 c2f1.png|center|332px]] {{c|Diagram of Roman Toga (according to Müller, in "Philologus").}} {{smaller block|On a Marble . . . is the Effigies of a Man ''Togated.'' {{right|''Ashmole'', Berkshire, I. 146.}}}} {{smaller block|The University, the mother of ''togated'' Peace. {{right|''Wood'', Fasti Oxon., II. (''Richardson.'')}}}} Hence—2. Stately; majestic. {{smaller block|What homebred English could ape the high Roman fashion of such ''togated'' words as "The multitudinous sea incarnadine"? {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 161.}}}} '''toge†''' (tōg), ''n.'' [ME. *''toge'' or ''togue'' (see the first quot.); < OF. ''toge'', ''togue'', F. ''toge'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''toga'', < L. ''toga'', togȧ: see ''toga''.] A toga. {{smaller block|Alle with taghte mene and towne in ''togers'' [read ''toges''? ''togues''?] fulle ryche, Of saunke realle in suyte, sexty [Romaynes] at ones. {{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 178.}}}} {{smaller block|Why in this woolvish ''toge'' should I stand here, To beg of Hob and Dick, that do appear, Their needless vouches? ''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 3. 122.}} {{smaller block|[The above is a modern reading; in the first folio the reading is ''tongue''; later folios have ''gown''. Compare ''toged''.]}} '''toged''' (tō′ged), ''a.'' [< ''toge'' + -''ed''2.] Clad in a toga; togated. {{smaller block|The bookish theoric, Wherein the ''toged'' consuls can propose As masterly as he. ''Shak.'', Othello, i. 1. 25.}} {{smaller block|[The first quarto has the above reading; the rest of the later editions have ''tongued''.]}} '''togeder†''', '''togedre†''', ''adv.'' Obsolete forms of ''together.'' '''togeman†''', '''togman†''' (tōg′-, tog′ma̤n), ''n.'' [< ''tog''2 + ''man.''] A cloak. {{smaller block|Sometime shall come in some Rogue, some picking knave, a Nimble Prig, . . . and plucketh off as many garments as be ought worth, that he may come by, and worth money, and . . . maketh port sale at some convenient place of theirs, that some be soon ready in the morning, for want of their Casters and ''Togemans.'' {{right|''Harman,'' Caveat for Cursetors, p. 105.}}}} '''together''' (tọ̈-geᴛ̵ʜ′ėr), ''adv.'' [Formerly or dial. also ''togeder, togider, togither'' (Sc. ''thegither''); < ME. ''togeder, togedere, togedre, togidere, togidre, togadere,'' < AS. ''tōgædere, tōgædre, tōgeador,'' together, < ''tō,'' to, + ''geador, gador,'' at once, together: see ''gather.'' Cf. ''togethers.''] 1. In company; in conjunction; simultaneously. {{smaller block|Mercifully ordain that we may become aged ''together.'' {{right|Tobit viii. 7.}} The subject of two of them [panels of sculpture] is his [Maximilian's] confederacy with Henry the Eighth, and the wars they made ''together'' upon France. {{right|''Addison,'' Remarks on Italy (Works, ed. Bohn, I. 535).}} ''Together'' let us beat this ample field. {{right|''Pope,'' Essay on Man, i. 9.}}}} 2. In the same place; to the same place. {{smaller block|The kynges were sette ''to-geder'' at oon table. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 133.}} Crabbed age and youth cannot live ''together.'' {{right|''Shak.,'' Passionate Pilgrim, l. 157.}}}} 3. In the same time; contemporaneously. {{smaller block|While he and I live ''together,'' I shall not be thought the worst poet of the age. {{right|''Dryden,'' Pref. to Fables.}}}} 4. The one with the other; with each other; mutually. {{smaller block|Pilgrymes and palmers pliȝted hem ''togidere''
To seke seynt Iames and seyntes in rome. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), Prol., l. 46.}}}} {{smaller block|When two or more concepts are compared ''together'' according to their comprehension, they either coincide or they do not. {{right|''Sir W. Hamilton'', Logic, xii.}}}} 5. In or into combination, junction, or union; so as to unite or blend: as, to sew, knit, pin, bind, or yoke two things ''together''. {{smaller block|Kyng David . . . putte theise 2 Names [Jebus and Salem] ''to gidere'', and cleped it Jebusalem. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 73.}}}} {{smaller block|What therefore God hath joined ''together'', let no man put asunder. {{right|Mat. xix. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|I'll manacle thy neck and feet ''together''. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 461.}}}} {{smaller block|The small faction which had been held ''together'' by the influence and promises of Prince Frederic had been dispersed by his death. {{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Clive.}}}} 6. Without intermission; uninterruptedly; on end. {{smaller block|Can you sit seven hours ''together'', and say nothing? {{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, ii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|It has been said in the praise of some men that they could talk whole hours ''together'' upon anything. {{right|''Addison'', Lady Orators.}}}} '''To consist, get, hang,''' etc., '''together.''' [< ME. ''togederes''; < ''together'' + adverbial gen. ''-es''.] Same as ''together''. {{smaller block|The next day he assembled all the Captaines of his army ''togethers''. {{right|''J.
